title: A Warning at Bethel's Altar
overview: An unnamed prophet from Judah condemns King Jeroboam's rival altar at Bethel, then is deceived by an older prophet and dies for breaking the instructions he was given.

parts.label: A message against the altar (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Bethel was one of two shrines Jeroboam set up, with golden calf statues, so his northern kingdom would not go to worship at Jerusalem. The prophet predicts that a future king from David's family named Josiah will kill the shrine's priests on this altar and burn human bones there, which would make it unfit for worship, and he says the altar splitting open will be the proof.

parts.label: The king's hand (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Jeroboam points at the prophet and orders him seized, but his outstretched hand shrivels so he cannot pull it back, and the altar splits just as foretold. He begs the prophet to pray for him and his hand is restored, though he asks only for his hand, not for any change of course.

parts.label: Refusing the king's table (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Sharing a meal signaled friendship and acceptance, so refusing to eat or drink in Bethel showed that God did not approve of what was happening there. The text gives no reason for the order to take a different road home, and interpreters can only guess, perhaps to keep the trip a pure errand rather than a visit.

parts.label: The old prophet's lie (vv. 11-19)
parts.note: An older prophet living in Bethel rides after him and falsely claims an angel told him to bring the man home for a meal. The text says plainly that he lied but never says why, and readers have long debated whether he meant to test him, discredit him, or something else.

parts.label: Death on the road (vv. 20-25)
parts.note: At the table the liar suddenly speaks a true message from the LORD, announcing that his guest will not be buried with his family, and soon a lion kills the man on the road. The lion standing beside the body without eating it or attacking the donkey marks this as no ordinary attack, yet the story stays harsh: the deceived man dies while the deceiver lives.

parts.label: Burial and an unchanged king (vv. 26-34)
parts.note: The old prophet mourns the man, buries him in his own tomb, and asks to be laid beside him because he is sure the warning against Bethel will come true (2 Kings 23 later reports that Josiah left these bones undisturbed). Jeroboam keeps appointing anyone who wants the job as a priest at his shrines, and the writer names this as the reason his royal family was later wiped out.

disagreement: Christians differ over why the deceived prophet is punished so severely while the lying prophet is spared, some seeing a strict lesson about holding to what God has said and others finding the story's justice genuinely troubling or deliberately left unresolved.
think: When someone you trust tells you something that contradicts what you were sure of, how do you decide whom to believe?
